title: Scalable, Simple, and Versatile Encapsulation of 2D Materials and Devices
authors: Gabriel Natale, Uma Chirkova, Flávio Henriques Feres, Ran Jing, Michael Geiwitz, Wenyao Liu, Emma Low, Josh Leeman, Kyung-Mo Kim, Leslie M. Schoop, Mohamed Shehabeldin, Qiong Ma, Michael A. Susner, Pijush Bhattacharya, Genda Gu, Katherine Lee, James Hone, Mengkun Liu, Kenneth S. Burch
abstract: Air-sensitive 2D materials present a fundamental challenge for device integration. Encapsulation is often required to preserve intrinsic properties, yet conventional protection strategies often fail for thicker layers and complicate fabrication. Here, we demonstrate that electron-beam (e-beam) evaporated aluminum oxide ($\mathrm{AlO}_x$) serves as both an effective encapsulation layer and a platform for direct device fabrication. Unlike transfer-based approaches, this scalable method is compatible with thicker flakes and full device or wafer coverage. It requires no stacking procedures and enables contacts without post-encapsulation etching. Using rare-earth tritellurides ($\mathrm{RTe}_3$, R = La, Er), semimetallic $\mathrm{WTe}_2$, and superconducting $\mathrm{FeTe}_x\mathrm{Se}_{1-x}$, we show that $\mathrm{AlO}_x$ suppresses oxidation and preserves intrinsic optical and electronic properties. We establish substrate-dependent optimization of encapsulation across a range of flake thicknesses, demonstrate that ultrathin $\mathrm{AlO}_x$ preserves $\mathrm{WTe}_2$'s plasmonic response and maintains superconducting performance in $\mathrm{FeTe}_x\mathrm{Se}_{1-x}$. Thus we overcome the longstanding tradeoff between encapsulation and straightforward device fabrication in fragile quantum materials.
summary: This work introduces e-beam evaporated aluminum oxide (AlOx) as a superior, scalable encapsulation method for highly air-sensitive 2D quantum materials. By demonstrating that AlOx preserves the electronic and optical properties of materials like WTe2 and superconducting FeTeSe, the authors resolve a major bottleneck in fabricating functional quantum devices.
main_problem: Air-sensitive 2D materials are difficult to integrate into functional devices due to environmental degradation and complex fabrication requirements.
main_result: Electron-beam evaporated aluminum oxide (AlOx) serves as a scalable, simple encapsulation layer that preserves the intrinsic electronic and optical properties of various 2D materials, enabling straightforward device fabrication.
method: The authors used e-beam evaporation to deposit AlOx over 2D materials and characterized the results using Raman spectroscopy, s-SNOM, and electrical transport measurements.
model_or_system: The study focuses on several 2D materials, including rare-earth tritellurides (RTe3), semimetallic WTe2, and superconducting iron-based compounds (FeTe_xSe_{1-x}). These materials are tested both in their pristine state and after encapsulation.
key_observables: Oxidation peaks (TeOx) in Raman spectra, plasmonic response contrast via s-SNOM, superconducting critical temperature (Tc) from R vs T measurements, and preservation of intrinsic optical/electronic properties.
important_parameters: AlOx thickness (e.g., 3 nm, 130 nm), flake thickness, temperature range (low T for superconductivity), and substrate type (SiO2 vs. Al2O3).
main_assumptions: The method overcomes the traditional trade-off between effective encapsulation and simple, scalable device fabrication procedures.
figures_summary: Figures show Raman spectra comparing encapsulated vs. uncapped flakes (demonstrating oxidation suppression), s-SNOM images showing preserved optical contrast through AlOx, and R vs T curves confirming superconductivity in encapsulated devices.
paper_structure: The paper systematically demonstrates the protective capability of AlOx using RTe3 (Raman analysis), then validates its compatibility with optical probing (s-SNOM on WTe2), and finally proves its utility in device fabrication by maintaining superconductivity in FeTeSe.
why_interesting: While primarily materials science, the ability to precisely control the environment and interface chemistry of quantum materials using a scalable deposition technique is crucial for realizing any quantum device, linking directly to open quantum system engineering.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Evolution of thin (tflake < 30 nm) LaTe3 and ErTe3 flakes with exposure to the ambient environment measured via Raman spectra normalized to the lowest energy, intrinsic phonon. The flakes without AlOx capping (a,c,e) reveal a rapid and continued enhancement of the TeOx peaks (black arrows), while the AlOx coated flakes (b,d,f) remain unchanged. Insets in a-d display the AFM topography of the flakes, revealing that encapsulated flakes remain uniform, whereas flakes without AlOx capping exhibit a rough surface and interlayer delamination.

Figure 2: The impact of substrate choice on edge encapsulation quality is demonstrated by com- paring the evolution of LaTe3 Raman spectra normalized to the lowest energy phonon mode for flakes with tflake ≥45 nm on a) SiO2 and b) sapphire (Al2O3) substrates. c) Ratio of the integrated intensity of the TeOx-related mode (130 cm−1) to the lowest energy LaTe3 mode (92 cm−1) vs flake thickness for 37 measurement points across 26 unique flakes.

Figure 3: Protection and impact of AlOx deposition on WTe2. a) Optical microscopy image of the WTe2 flake on SiO2 substrate after AlOx deposition. b) AFM/topography image and c) 1550 cm−1 s-SNOM image performed in the white dashed highlighted area. The blue and red dashed lines indicate the spatial profiles displayed in d) AFM topography (top) and near-field optical image (bottom). e) Optical microscopy image of an exfoliated WTe2 flake on SiO2 substrate after AlOx deposition with point spectra locations marked in thick (P1) and thin (P2) regions. f) Thick and g) thin region WTe2 Raman spectra normalized to the peak located at 167 cm−1, plotted before (blue) and after (red) AlOx deposition.

Figure 4: Resistance (blue) and dR/dT (red) vs temperature with device images shown in the inset for a) FeTe0.55Se0.45 fabricated using photolithography followed by encapsulation b) FeTe0.55Se0.45 fabricated directly through a 3 nm sacrificial AlOx layer without subsequent thick encapsulation and c) FeTe0.70Se0.30 fabricated using t-SPL followed by encapsulation. Dashed lines mark the peak position in dR/dT, and thus Tc.
